newsitem.title: GERMANY: Jochimsen-EMU delay talk should be shelved till 98.
newsitem.headline: Jochimsen-EMU delay talk should be shelved till 98.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Reimut Jochimsen said on Monday it was premature to talk about possible delays in European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and debate on the issue should be shelved until the selection process actually begins.

The approach of 1998 -- the year for deciding which EU members qualify to launch a single currency -- was putting pressure on countries to meet the requirements, so it would be bad to talk about timing now, Jochimsen said.
But if it was clear then that not enough EU candidates would be able to qualify by the January 1999 launch date, it should be postponed by a precisely defined period, Jochimsen said.

"I think a decision on a possible later start date should only be taken when the selection procedure is actually on the agenda," Jochimsen told a a public hearing organised by the state parliament of North Rhine-Westphalia.
"That means not currently, only when time pressure is at last triggering quality pressure."
Jochimsen, who is president of the state central bank of North Rhine-Westphalia, rejected the idea of loosening the entry conditions for monetary union to allow more countries in.
"Under no circumstances can there be any question of a softening of convergence criteria," Jochimsen said. Delving into such a "box of tricks" would be politically convenient but extremely risky.
Monetary union was desirable from an economic and political point of view but the Euro would have to be built on such a solid foundation that it would be as strong as the mark.

An overhasty launch by partners that were not ready for it would have the disastrous effect of creating an inflationary community, Jochimsen said. It was also important to set up mechanisms to ensure that partners continued to meet the criteria after the launch of EMU.

Europe's top financial officials this weekend came closer to creating such a mechanism by clearing key hurdles in their quest for a stability pact to control public spending once countries enter monetary union. But they failed to agree exactly how the pact would work.

European Union finance ministers and central bank governors said at the end of informal one-day talks in Dublin, Ireland, on Saturday that the broad outline of plans to punish governments that exceeded certain budget deficit limits were now in place.
But specifics of the plan -- including the size of fines to be levied on offenders -- were referred to committees in the hope a consensus could be thrashed out by the end of the year.
